answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Tennyson wrote this exact line in Canto XXVII of ‘In Memoriam A. H. H.’ (1850), his long elegy for his friend Arthur Henry Hallam. The wording — ‘’Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all’ — is genuine and appears verbatim in the published poem.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
I hold it true, whate’er befall;
I feel it when I sorrow most;
’Tis better to have loved and lost
Than never to have loved at all.
trail: The couplet closes Canto XXVII of Tennyson’s In Memoriam A. H. H., first published in 1850.
The elegy mourns Arthur Henry Hallam, Tennyson’s Cambridge friend, who died suddenly in 1833 at twenty-two.
Tennyson coined the modern phrasing, though kindred sentiments appear earlier — e.g. Congreve’s 1700 play The Way of the World.
source.excerptNote: The complete closing stanza of Canto XXVII. The famous line is the third of these four; it is almost always quoted on its own.

source.rightsNote: In Memoriam A. H. H. was first published in 1850, long before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, and Tennyson died in 1892. The poem — and this line — are firmly in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
author.heading: About Alfred, Lord Tennyson
author.bio: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was Poet Laureate of Great Britain and Ireland for most of Queen Victoria’s reign and the most popular poet of the Victorian era. In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850), a sequence of 131 short cantos written over seventeen years, mourns his friend Arthur Henry Hallam and helped secure his appointment as Laureate that same year. He also gave the language “Theirs not to reason why” and “Nature, red in tooth and claw.”

misattribution.heading: Wait — but there’s a catch
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Tennyson is correct. What people get wrong is the surrounding folklore — who to credit, and a famous parody often mistaken for the real thing.

items.why: The line is sometimes tossed to Shakespeare or an ancient sage online. It is neither — it is Tennyson’s, from In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850).

Kindred sentiments predate Tennyson — Congreve’s The Way of the World (1700): “’tis better to be left than never to have loved,” and Wollstonecraft (1792) on being “disappointed in love, than never to love.” But the exact modern phrasing is Tennyson’s own.
“’Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have lost at all” is Samuel Butler’s satirical twist — a joke on Tennyson, not the original line. The genuine Tennyson keeps ‘loved’ in both halves.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is authentically Tennyson’s — the closing couplet of Canto XXVII of In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Tennyson began In Memoriam in the raw grief after Arthur Henry Hallam — his closest friend and his sister’s fiancé — died of a brain hemorrhage in Vienna in 1833, aged twenty-two. The poem took him roughly seventeen years, moving from despair toward a hard-won faith.

Canto XXVII lands on the line that has since become one of the most quoted consolations in English: the claim that love, even ending in loss, is worth the grief. Published in 1850, the sequence was an immediate success and helped win Tennyson the Poet Laureateship that year.
